transcript.text: induction hob keeps turnin off after 5-10 mins on high, have to keep restartin it. drives me nuts. any1 know y?

Common reasons an induction hob shuts off after 5–10 mins on high:

• Overheating protection – most likely. The cooling fan/air vents underneath may be blocked, filters dirty, or the hob may not have enough ventilation in the cabinet. Let it cool, check nothing is blocking vents, and listen for the fan.
• “Boost”/Power Boost mode timing out – many hobs only allow boost for a few minutes, then automatically drop to a lower setting. It shouldn’t normally fully switch off though.
• Pan issue – a warped, too-small, non-magnetic, or badly centred pan can make it lose detection when hot. Try a different flat magnetic pan on another zone.
• Heat from the pan affecting controls – very large pans or steam can overheat/touch the control area. Keep handles/pans away from the touch panel and wipe it dry.
• Electrical/installation fault – if all rings cut out, especially with no error code, it could be supply wiring, a loose connection, or the hob itself.

Try using it on high but not Boost, with a different pan, and check whether only one ring does it or the whole hob. If it shows an error code, note it down.

If it keeps completely shutting down, or you smell burning / see flickering / the breaker trips, stop using it and get the manufacturer’s engineer or a qualified electrician to inspect it—don’t open the hob yourself.
its mostly the big front rings on high. fan roars before it cuts out. comes back after a few mins. started after new drawer unit fitted under it last month

That strongly points to overheating from reduced ventilation under the hob. The loud fan is it trying to cool itself; the cut-out and restart after a few minutes is the thermal safety protection kicking in.

Since it started right after the drawer unit went in, likely causes are:

• Drawer/cabinet is too close to the underside of the hob
• The required air gap or ventilation opening has been blocked
• A solid drawer top/back panel is trapping hot air
• Drawer contents are blocking the ventilation space
• The installer hasn’t fitted the required separator/heat shield panel, if your hob’s instructions require one

The large front zones create the most heat, so they’re often the first to trigger it.

What to do:
1. Check the hob installation manual for the required clearance and ventilation dimensions beneath it.
2. Pull the drawer out completely and see whether the hob behaves normally on high with the drawer removed. If it does, that’s very good evidence the new unit is restricting airflow.
3. Don’t keep repeatedly running it until it cuts out — use lower settings for now.
4. Get the kitchen fitter/installer back to correct the cabinet ventilation. This may mean lowering the drawer, adding vents/openings, changing the drawer box, or fitting a heat-deflector panel as specified by the hob manufacturer.

Don’t block vents with cutlery, foil, manuals etc., and don’t modify wiring or open the hob. If it still does it with the drawer removed and clear airflow underneath, arrange a hob service visit instead.
not pulling the drawer out, not doing that. so is it the fitter's fault then? just want it sorted

Very likely, yes — especially as it began immediately after the new drawer unit was fitted.

The fitter may have reduced or blocked the ventilation clearance the hob needs underneath. Induction hobs need airflow for their electronics, and the roaring fan + cooling-down period before it works again is classic overheating protection.

Contact the fitter and say something like:

> “Since the drawer unit was installed under the induction hob, the large front zones shut down after 5–10 minutes on high. The cooling fan runs loudly and it works again once cooled. Please check the hob manufacturer’s required under-hob ventilation clearances, drawer position and any heat-shield/separator requirements, and rectify the installation.”

Ask them to compare the actual installation against the hob’s installation manual—not just say “there’s a drawer underneath, it’s fine.” The fix is usually altering the drawer/cabinet or adding the specified ventilation/deflector arrangement, rather than replacing the hob.

If the drawer unit was fitted exactly to the manufacturer’s installation requirements, then it may be a hob/fan fault—but based on the timing, the altered cabinet ventilation is the obvious first thing to investigate.
